claim: Stxbp1/Munc18-1 is an essential component of the presynaptic neurotransmitter release machinery.
source: Syntaxin-binding protein 1 (STXBP1, also known as MUNC18-1) is an essential component of the presynaptic neurotransmitter release machinery.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about STXBP1.

claim: De novo heterozygous pathogenic variants in STXBP1 are among the most frequent causes of neurodevelopmental disorders including intellectual disabilities and epilepsies.
source: De novo heterozygous pathogenic variants in STXBP1 are among the most frequent causes of neurodevelopmental disorders including intellectual disabilities and epilepsies.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Stxbp1 haploinsufficiency caused cognitive, psychiatric, and motor dysfunctions in mice.
source: Here we modeled STXBP1 encephalopathy in mice and found that Stxbp1 haploinsufficiency caused cognitive, psychiatric, and motor dysfunctions, as well as cortical hyperexcitability and seizures.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by extensive behavioral testing data presented in Figures 2-5.

claim: Stxbp1 haploinsufficiency caused cortical hyperexcitability and seizures in mice.
source: Here we modeled STXBP1 encephalopathy in mice and found that Stxbp1 haploinsufficiency caused cognitive, psychiatric, and motor dysfunctions, as well as cortical hyperexcitability and seizures.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by EEG/EMG data in Figure 6.

claim: Stxbp1 haploinsufficiency reduced cortical inhibitory neurotransmission via distinct mechanisms from parvalbumin-expressing and somatostatin-expressing interneurons.
source: Furthermore, Stxbp1 haploinsufficiency reduced cortical inhibitory neurotransmission via distinct mechanisms from parvalbumin-expressing and somatostatin-expressing interneurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by electrophysiology data in Figures 8 and 9.

claim: Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice recapitulate cardinal features of STXBP1 encephalopathy.
source: These results demonstrate that Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice recapitulate cardinal features of STXBP1 encephalopathy and indicate that GABAergic synaptic dysfunction is likely a crucial contributor to disease pathogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the comprehensive phenotypic characterization presented in the results.

claim: GABAergic synaptic dysfunction is likely a crucial contributor to STXBP1 encephalopathy pathogenesis.
source: These results demonstrate that Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice recapitulate cardinal features of STXBP1 encephalopathy and indicate that GABAergic synaptic dysfunction is likely a crucial contributor to disease pathogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the finding of reduced inhibitory transmission from Pv and Sst interneurons.

claim: Stxbp1/Munc18-1 is involved in synaptic vesicle docking, priming, and fusion through multiple interactions with neuronal SNAREs.
source: Stxbp1/Munc18-1 is involved in synaptic vesicle docking, priming, and fusion through multiple interactions with the neuronal soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor-attachment protein receptors (SNAREs) (Rizo and Xu, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Genetic deletion of Stxbp1 in worms, flies, mice, and fish abolishes neurotransmitter release and leads to lethality and cell-intrinsic degeneration of neurons.
source: Genetic deletion of Stxbp1 in worms, flies, mice, and fish abolishes neurotransmitter release and leads to lethality and cell-intrinsic degeneration of neurons (Harrison et al., 1994; Verhage, 2000; Weimer et al., 2003; Heeroma et al., 2004; Grone et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction with multiple citations supporting it.

claim: STXBP1 de novo heterozygous mutations cause several of the most severe forms of epileptic encephalopathies including Ohtahara syndrome.
source: In humans, STXBP1 de novo heterozygous mutations cause several of the most severe forms of epileptic encephalopathies including Ohtahara syndrome (Saitsu et al., 2008; Saitsu et al., 2010), West syndrome (Deprez et al., 2010; Otsuka et al., 2010), Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (Carvill et al., 2013; Allen et al., 2013), Dravet syndrome (Carvill et al., 2014), and other types of early-onset epileptic encephalopathies (Deprez et al., 2010; Mignot et al., 2011; Stamberger et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction with citations supporting each syndrome mentioned.

claim: STXBP1 is one of the most frequently mutated genes in sporadic intellectual disabilities and developmental disorders.
source: Furthermore, STXBP1 is one of the most frequently mutated genes in sporadic intellectual disabilities and developmental disorders (Hamdan et al., 2009; Hamdan et al., 2011; Rauch et al., 2012; Deciphering Developmental Disorders Study, 2015; Deciphering Developmental Disorders Study, 2017; Suri et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction with multiple citations supporting it.

claim: All STXBP1 encephalopathy patients show intellectual disability, mostly severe to profound.
source: All STXBP1 encephalopathy patients show intellectual disability, mostly severe to profound, and 95% of patients have epilepsy (Stamberger et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction with a citation supporting it.

claim: 95% of STXBP1 encephalopathy patients have epilepsy.
source: All STXBP1 encephalopathy patients show intellectual disability, mostly severe to profound, and 95% of patients have epilepsy (Stamberger et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction with a citation supporting it.

claim: More than 90% of STXBP1 encephalopathy patients have motor deficits, such as dystonia, spasticity, ataxia, hypotonia, and tremor.
source: More than 90% of patients have motor deficits, such as dystonia, spasticity, ataxia, hypotonia, and tremor.
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: STXBP1 encephalopathy is mostly caused by haploinsufficiency because more than 60% of the reported mutations are either deletions, nonsense, frameshift, or splice site variants.
source: STXBP1 encephalopathy is mostly caused by haploinsufficiency because more than 60% of the reported mutations are either deletions, nonsense, frameshift, or splice site variants (Stamberger et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction with a citation supporting it.

claim: A subset of STXBP1 missense variants were shown to destabilize the protein.
source: A subset of missense variants were shown to destabilize the protein (Saitsu et al., 2008; Saitsu et al., 2010; Guiberson et al., 2018; Kovacevic et al., 2018) and cause aggregation to further reduce the wild type (WT) protein levels (Guiberson et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction with citations supporting it.

claim: Removing stxbp1b, one of the two STXBP1 homologs in zebrafish, caused spontaneous electrographic seizures.
source: Indeed, removing stxbp1b, one of the two STXBP1 homologs in zebrafish, caused spontaneous electrographic seizures (Grone et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction with a citation supporting it.

claim: Three different Stxbp1 null alleles have been generated in mice.
source: Three different Stxbp1 null alleles have been generated in mice (Verhage, 2000; Miyamoto et al., 2017; Kovacevic et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction with citations supporting it.

claim: Stxbp1 protein levels were reduced by only 25% in the brain of one line of previous Stxbp1 heterozygous knockout mice.
source: Interestingly, Stxbp1 protein levels were reduced by only 25% in the brain of one line of previous Stxbp1 heterozygous knockout mice (Orock et al., 2018) and 25% in the cortex and 50% in the hippocampus of another line (Miyamoto et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction with citations supporting it.

claim: Stxbp1 protein levels were reduced by 25% in the cortex and 50% in the hippocampus of another line of Stxbp1 heterozygous knockout mice.
source: Interestingly, Stxbp1 protein levels were reduced by only 25% in the brain of one line of previous Stxbp1 heterozygous knockout mice (Orock et al., 2018) and 25% in the cortex and 50% in the hippocampus of another line (Miyamoto et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction with citations supporting it.

claim: Homozygous mutants (Stxbp1tm1d/tm1d and Stxbp1tm1a/tm1a) died immediately after birth because they were completely paralyzed and could not breathe.
source: Homozygous mutants (Stxbp1tm1d/tm1d and Stxbp1tm1a/tm1a) died immediately after birth because they were completely paralyzed and could not breathe, consistent with the previous Stxbp1 null alleles (Verhage, 2000; Miyamoto et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and is supported by observation of the mice and citations to previous studies.

claim: At embryonic day 17.5, Stxbp1 protein was absent in Stxbp1tm1d/tm1d and Stxbp1tm1a/tm1a mice, and reduced by 50% in Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice.
source: Western blots with antibodies recognizing either the N- or C-terminus of Stxbp1 showed that at embryonic day 17.5, Stxbp1 protein was absent in Stxbp1tm1d/tm1d and Stxbp1tm1a/tm1a mice, and reduced by 50% in Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C), indicating that both tm1d and tm1a are null alleles.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Both tm1d and tm1a are null alleles.
source: Western blots with antibodies recognizing either the N- or C-terminus of Stxbp1 showed that at embryonic day 17.5, Stxbp1 protein was absent in Stxbp1tm1d/tm1d and Stxbp1tm1a/tm1a mice, and reduced by 50% in Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C), indicating that both tm1d and tm1a are null alleles.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on Western blot data showing absence of protein in homozygous mutants.

claim: Stxbp1 was reduced by 40–50% in most brain areas of Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice at 3 months of age except the cerebellum and olfactory bulb where the reduction was 20–30%.
source: We surveyed the Stxbp1 protein levels in different brain regions of Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice at 3 months of age. Stxbp1 was reduced by 40–50% in most brain areas except the cerebellum and olfactory bulb where the reduction was 20–30% (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ are Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice.
source: These results demonstrate that Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ are indeed Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the Western blot data showing reduced protein levels.

claim: At the time of genotyping (around postnatal week 3), Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice are 40% and 43% of the total offspring, respectively, indicating a postnatal lethality phenotype.
source: We bred Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice with WT mice and found that at the time of genotyping (i.e., around postnatal week 3) Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice are 40% and 43% of the total offspring, respectively (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), indicating a postnatal lethality phenotype.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by genotyping data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice show reduced survival, but this phenotype is not fully penetrant.
source: Thus, Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice show reduced survival, but this phenotype is not fully penetrant.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the survival data.

claim: The body weights of Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice were consistently about 20% less than their sex- and age-matched WT littermates.
source: Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice appeared smaller and their body weights were consistently about 20% less than their sex- and age-matched WT littermates (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by body weight data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: At 4 weeks of age, Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice began to exhibit abnormal hindlimb clasping, indicative of dystonia or spasticity.
source: At 4 weeks of age, Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice began to exhibit abnormal hindlimb clasping, indicative of dystonia or spasticity (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1E and 1G.

claim: By the age of 3 months, almost all Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice developed hindlimb clasping.
source: By the age of 3 months, almost all mutant mice developed hindlimb clasping (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice traveled longer distances and faster than WT mice in the open-field test, indicating that Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice are hyperactive.
source: The locomotion of Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice was largely normal, but they traveled longer distances and faster than WT mice, indicating that Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice are hyperactive (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by open-field test data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice explored the center region of the arena less than WT mice and made less vertical movements, indicating that the mutant mice are more anxious.
source: Both Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice explored the center region of the arena less than WT mice (Figure 2D) and made less vertical movements (Figure 2E), indicating that the mutant mice are more anxious.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by open-field test data shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: The forelimb grip strength of Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice was weaker than WT mice.
source: However, the forelimb grip strength of Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice was weaker (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by grip strength test data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: In the foot slip test, both Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice made many more foot slips than WT mice.
source: Furthermore, in the foot slip test where a mouse is allowed to walk on a wire grid, both Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice were not able to place their paws precisely on the wire to hold themselves and made many more foot slips than WT mice (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by foot slip test data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: In the vertical pole test, it took Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice longer to orient themselves downward and descend the pole than WT mice.
source: To assess the agility of mice, we performed the vertical pole test, which is often used to measure the bradykinesia of parkinsonism. When mice were placed head-up on the top of a vertical pole, it took mutant mice longer to orient themselves downward and descend the pole than WT mice (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by vertical pole test data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice do not develop ataxia, but their fine motor coordination and muscle strength are reduced.
source: Together, these results indicate that Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice do not develop ataxia, but their fine motor coordination and muscle strength are reduced.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the motor function tests.

claim: Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice showed normal startle responses to different levels of sound.
source: We next examined the acoustic sensory function and found that Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice showed normal startle responses to different levels of sound (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by acoustic startle test data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice displayed similar pre-pulse inhibition as WT mice.
source: To test sensorimotor gating, we measured the pre-pulse inhibition where the startle response to a strong sound is reduced by a preceding weaker sound. Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice displayed similar pre-pulse inhibition as WT mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by pre-pulse inhibition test data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice had normal nociception as measured by the hot plate test.
source: They also had normal nociception as measured by the hot plate test (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by hot plate test data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The sensory functions and sensorimotor gating of Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice are normal.
source: Thus, the sensory functions and sensorimotor gating of Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice are normal.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the sensory function tests.

claim: When tested with an inter-trial interval of 24 hr in the novel object recognition test, WT mice interacted more with the novel object than the familiar object, whereas Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice interacted equally between the familiar and novel objects.
source: When tested with an inter-trial interval of 24 hr, WT mice interacted more with the novel object than the familiar object, whereas Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice interacted equally between the familiar and novel objects (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by novel object recognition test data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Both long-term and short-term recognition memories are impaired in Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice.
source: Thus, both long-term and short-term recognition memories are impaired in Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the novel object recognition test data with different inter-trial intervals.

claim: At two tested ages, Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice displayed a profound reduction in both context- and cue-induced freezing behaviors when tested 24 hr after the fear conditioning paradigm.
source: At two tested ages, Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice displayed a profound reduction in both context- and cue-induced freezing behaviors when tested 24 hr after the conditioning paradigm (Figure 3B–E).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by fear conditioning test data shown in Figure 3B–E.

claim: Stxbp1 haploinsufficiency impairs both hippocampus-dependent contextual and hippocampus-independent cued fear memories.
source: Since the acoustic startle response and nociception are intact in Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,C), these results indicate that Stxbp1 haploinsufficiency impairs both hippocampus-dependent contextual and hippocampus-independent cued fear memories.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the fear conditioning test data and the normal sensory functions.

claim: Both long-term and short-term forms of recognition and associative memories are severely impaired in Stxbp1 haploinsufficiency mice, but their working memory is intact.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that both long-term and short-term forms of recognition and associative memories are severely impaired in Stxbp1 haploinsufficiency mice, but their working memory is intact.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the cognitive function tests.

claim: In the elevated plus maze test, Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice entered the open arms less frequently and traveled shorter distance in the open arms than WT mice.
source: Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice entered the open arms and clear chamber less frequently and traveled shorter distance in the open arms and clear chamber than WT mice (Figure 4A–D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by elevated plus maze test data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: In the light-dark chamber test, Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice made less transitions between the light and dark chambers and traveled shorter distance in the light chamber than WT mice.
source: Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice entered the open arms and clear chamber less frequently and traveled shorter distance in the open arms and clear chamber than WT mice (Figure 4A–D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by light-dark chamber test data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: The elevated plus maze and light-dark chamber tests confirm the heightened anxiety in Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice.
source: Hence, these results confirm the heightened anxiety in Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice and are consistent with the previous studies (Hager et al., 2014; Miyamoto et al., 2017; Kovacevic et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the anxiety tests and is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the hole-board test, Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice made more repetitive nose pokes than WT mice across many holes.
source: We analyzed the repetitive nose pokes (i.e.,≥2 consecutive pokes) into the same hole as a measure of repetitive behaviors. The mutant mice made more repetitive nose pokes than WT mice across many holes (Figure 4G), indicating that Stxbp1 haploinsufficiency in mice causes abnormal stereotypy and repetitive behaviors, a psychiatric feature observed in about 20% of the STXBP1 encephalopathy patients (Stamberger et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by hole-board test data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Stxbp1 haploinsufficiency in mice causes abnormal stereotypy and repetitive behaviors.
source: We analyzed the repetitive nose pokes (i.e.,≥2 consecutive pokes) into the same hole as a measure of repetitive behaviors. The mutant mice made more repetitive nose pokes than WT mice across many holes (Figure 4G), indicating that Stxbp1 haploinsufficiency in mice causes abnormal stereotypy and repetitive behaviors, a psychiatric feature observed in about 20% of the STXBP1 encephalopathy patients (Stamberger et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the hole-board test data.

claim: In the resident-intruder test, male resident Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice were more likely to attack and spent more time attacking the intruders as compared to WT mice.
source: As compared to WT mice, male resident Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice were more likely to attack and spent more time attacking the intruders (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by resident-intruder test data shown in Figure 5A–C.

claim: In the tube test, when Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice were placed against their sex- and age-matched WT littermates, Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice won more competitions despite their smaller body sizes.
source: Another paradigm to assess aggression and social dominance is the tube test, in which two mice are released into the opposite ends of a tube, and the more dominant and aggressive mouse will win the competition by pushing its opponent out of the tube. When Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice were placed against their sex- and age-matched WT littermates, Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice won more competitions despite their smaller body sizes (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by tube test data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Stxbp1 haploinsufficiency elevates innate aggression in mice.
source: Thus, Stxbp1 haploinsufficiency elevates innate aggression in mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the aggression tests.

claim: In the three-chamber test, like WT mice, Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice preferred to interact with the partner mice rather than the objects.
source: Like WT mice, Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice preferred to interact with the partner mice rather than the objects (Figure 5E), indicating that Stxbp1 haploinsufficiency does not compromise general sociability.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by three-chamber test data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Stxbp1 haploinsufficiency does not compromise general sociability.
source: Like WT mice, Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice preferred to interact with the partner mice rather than the objects (Figure 5E), indicating that Stxbp1 haploinsufficiency does not compromise general sociability.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the three-chamber test data.

claim: In the partition test, both WT and Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice preferentially interacted more with the novel partner mice.
source: Furthermore, we used the partition test to examine the preference for social novelty, in which a mouse is allowed to interact with a familiar or novel partner mouse. Both WT and Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice preferentially interacted more with the novel partner mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by partition test data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The general sociability and interest in social novelty are normal in Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice.
source: These results indicate that the general sociability and interest in social novelty are normal in Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the social interaction tests.

claim: In the Nestlet shredding test, Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice consistently scored lower than WT mice at all time points.
source: We provided a Nestlet (pressed cotton square) to each mouse in the home cage and scored the degree of shredding and nest quality after 24, 48, and 72 hr (Figure 5F). Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice consistently scored lower than WT mice at all time points (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by Nestlet shredding test data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: In the marble burying test, Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice buried fewer marbles than WT mice.
source: In the marble burying test, the Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice buried fewer marbles than WT mice (Figure 5H).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by marble burying test data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice exhibited cortical hyperexcitability and several epileptiform activities.
source: Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice exhibited cortical hyperexcitability and several epileptiform activities.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and is supported by EEG/EMG data in Figure 6.

claim: Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice had numerous spike-wave discharges (SWDs) that typically were 3–6 Hz and lasted 1–2 s.
source: First, they had numerous spike-wave discharges (SWDs) that typically were 3–6 Hz and lasted 1–2 s (Figure 6C,E,F).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by EEG data shown in Figure 6C,E,F.

claim: The frequency of SWD episodes in Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice was more than 40-fold higher than that in WT mice.
source: On average, the frequency of SWD episodes in Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice was more than 40-fold higher than that in WT mice (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by EEG data shown in Figure 6E,F.

claim: SWDs frequently occurred in a cluster manner in Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice, which never occurred in WT mice.
source: Importantly, SWDs frequently occurred in a cluster manner (i.e.,≥5 episodes with an inter-episode-interval of ≤60 s) in Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice, which never occurred in WT mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; Video 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by EEG data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Video 1.

claim: 56 episodes of SWDs from 10 out of 13 Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice lasted more than 4 s, among which 54 episodes occurred during REM sleep.
source: Furthermore, 56 episodes of SWDs from 10 out of 13 Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice lasted more than 4 s, among which 54 episodes occurred during rapid eye movement (REM) sleep (Figure 6D; Video 2) and the other two episodes occurred when mice were awake.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by EEG data shown in Figure 6D and Video 2.

claim: Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice experienced frequent myoclonic seizures that manifested as sudden jumps or more subtle, involuntary muscle jerks associated with EEG discharges.
source: Second, Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice experienced frequent myoclonic seizures that manifested as sudden jumps or more subtle, involuntary muscle jerks associated with EEG discharges (Figure 6G,H).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by EEG/EMG data shown in Figure 6G,H.

claim: Myoclonic jumps were observed in all 13 recorded Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice and the majority of episodes occurred during REM or NREM sleep.
source: The large movement artifacts associated with the myoclonic jumps precluded proper interpretation of EEG signals, but this type of myoclonic seizures was observed in all 13 recorded Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice and the majority of episodes occurred during REM or non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep (Figure 6I; Video 3).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by EEG/EMG data shown in Figure 6I and Video 3.

claim: The more subtle myoclonic jerks occurred frequently and often in clusters in Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice, whereas only isolated events were observed in WT mice at a much lower frequency.
source: Moreover, the more subtle myoclonic jerks occurred frequently and often in clusters in Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice, whereas only isolated events were observed in WT mice at a much lower frequency (Figure 6H,J; Video 4).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by EEG/EMG data shown in Figure 6H,J and Video 4.

claim: EEG and EMG recordings showed that the cortical EEG spikes associated with the myoclonic jerks occurred before or simultaneously with the neck muscle EMG discharges.
source: EEG and EMG recordings showed that the cortical EEG spikes associated with the myoclonic jerks occurred before or simultaneously with the neck muscle EMG discharges (Figure 6H), consistent with the cortical or subcortical origins of myoclonuses, respectively (Avanzini et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by EEG/EMG data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Immunostaining of a pan-neuronal marker NeuN revealed a grossly normal cytoarchitecture and cortical lamination in adult Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice.
source: Immunostaining of a pan-neuronal marker NeuN revealed a grossly normal cytoarchitecture and cortical lamination in adult Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: The densities of cortical neurons and two major classes of inhibitory neurons, Pv and Sst interneurons, were similar between Stxbp1tm1d/+ and WT mice.
source: The densities of cortical neurons and two major classes of inhibitory neurons, Pv and Sst interneurons, were similar between Stxbp1tm1d/+ and WT mice (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7B–D.
